title: K-number-based selection in Danish dachshunds: offspring outcomes and implications for genetic diversity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In dachshunds, the number of calcified discs (K-number [KN]) is one heritable determinant of the risk of intervertebral disc disease and is used for breeding selection in some countries; however, there are no prior reports of offspring KN outcomes or the effect of KN selection on size of the effective breeding population (Ne).

HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: To determine whether progressively limiting breeding eligibility to dogs with lower KNs would: (1) improve offspring KN outcomes and (2) reduce the effective population size of the breeding population below a threshold that risks genetic bottleneck.

ANIMALS: Danish dachshunds (n = 2120) with KN recorded to a public database from 1993 to 2024.

METHODS: This retrospective study analyzed KN records from 2120 dogs screened between 1990 and 2024. Associations between parental KN and offspring KN phenotype were evaluated using parent-offspring regression and cumulative-link ordinal models.

RESULTS: Worse offspring KN was predicted by both worse sire (P = 4.8 × 10-6; odds ratio [OR] 1.3; 95% CI, 1.16-1.45) and dam (P = 3.3 × 10-5; OR 1.3; 95% CI, 1.13-1.40) KN. Increasingly stringent parental KN selection was associated with improved offspring KN distributions, with predicted next-generation mean KN decreasing from 2.26 under K ≤ 4 selection to 1.54 under K0 selection. However, more stringent selection reduced effective breeding population size below thresholds associated with genetic bottleneck risk (eg, standard wirehaired: Ne = 179 under K ≤ 4 vs Ne = 52 under K0).

CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Increasingly stringent limitation of parent KN was associated with lower-KN offspring groups but also decreased effective population size, highlighting the need to balance disease-risk reduction against preservation of genetic diversity.
